My name is Mari Ant.
Hello, do you see me? I am the fourth ant in the line. Can you see me? My name is Mari Ant.
I may look very tiny to you, but I am very strong. Do you want to see how strong I am? Look at me lift this!
We ants like to walk in a line. We walk very quietly. Listen. Can you hear us walking? No. You cannot. We are very quiet.
We have a huge village. Hundreds of us live happily together. Ours is a very quiet little village.
We ants are not noisy like other animals. Dogs and cats and cows make noises. But we do not make noise. But we are very good at smelling. It is like smells are a language that tells us things.
One kind of smell says, “Follow me this way for a feast.”
But sometimes there is a different kind of smell. This smell tells me, “Danger! Do not go there!”
I love cakes and all kinds of sweets. Don't you? Mmmmm.
Never mind if the door is shut. I can slip through the smallest crack to get to food.

In his dream, he was flying.

pages.text:

“Fine, thank you,” Chandu replied.

pages.text:
Chandu flew a bit higher. Flying, flying. He flew into a sparrow.

“Hi there! How do you do?” she asked.

“Very well, thank you,” Chandu said.

image.alt: Flying boy with a sparrow

pages.text:
Then Chandu soared still higher. Flying, still flying, he met an eagle.

“Hello friend! How are you?” the eagle asked.

“I feel good,” replied Chandu.

image.alt: Flying boy with an eagle

pages.text:
Chandu was flying higher and higher. It seemed so easy. Flying, flying. So high that he came up to an aeroplane.

“Hey, Chandu, how do you do?” the aeroplane asked.

“Fine. And safe journey!” Chandu quickly replied.

image.alt: Flying boy with an aeroplane

pages.text:
Soon Chandu climbed higher than before. Flying and still flying.

A rocket came to meet him. “Hello sir, how do you do?” the rocket shouted.

“Very well,” Chandu smiled.

image.alt: Flying boy with a rocket

pages.text:
Still, Chandu was flying higher and higher. Now the stars were twinkling all around. They were smiling at Chandu, as though he were a part of them.

“How are you feeling Chandu?” one star asked him.

“I am feeling great!” he said.

Suddenly, the stars began to wobble. And shake.

image.alt: Flying boy with stars around him

pages.text:
It was Mother, shaking Chandu awake. “Good morning, how are you?”

He hugged her hard and said, “Oh, now I feel better than ever before!”

I sat on the floor. He sat on the chair.

Olwethu wants to play pretend.‌
“I want to fly like a bird, swim like a mermaid, roar like a lion,”
she tells Grandma.
But Grandma says, “Not now, Olwethu.
It’s time to go to school.”

STOMP! STOMP!
Olwethu’s feet go as she walks slowly to school.
But what is this?
There’s a door, covered in feathers. Olwethu walks up to it and…

WHOOSH!
Olwethu is a bird in the sky!

She’s flying!
Birds wave at her as they fly by.
ZOOOOM!

But what is this?
There’s another door, covered in scales.
FLAP!
FLAP!
She flies over, touches the door and…

SPLISH! SPLOSH!
Olwethu is a mermaid in the ocean!
The fish smile at her as she swims by.

But what is this?
There’s another door, shining bright like the sun.
She swims over, and…

“GRRRRRRRRR!”
Olwethu is a lion in the savannah.
She opens her mouth and…

“ROOOAAARRRR!”
Her voice is loud and powerful.
But what is this?
There’s another door, covered with photos of her friends.
She prowls over, holds up her paw, and…

WHIZZ!
Olwethu is herself again.
She’s in her classroom with her friends.

Teacher Songelwa says,
“HMMMMMM...
...where have you been, Olwethu?”

“WOW!
Teacher, I’ve been everywhere!”

pages.text:
Hello. My name is Poki.
I am Telu’s pig.
When Telu goes to school I have to stay at home.

Telu says that I am a clever pig.
I don’t want to stay at home. I want to go to school too.
One day I decided to follow Telu to school.

I went into the classroom.
I jumped up and sat on a chair.

"Oh look!" shouted a girl.
"It’s a pig!"
Telu turned around and saw me.
He shouted, "It’s Poki!"

"No pigs at school!" shouted the teacher.
I was scared.
I ran under a desk.

Everyone was shouting.
The children chased me around the classroom.
I jumped up on a desk and down again.

The children laughed.
One child cried.
Telu grabbed my tail.
I squealed.
"Now I’ve got you," said Telu. "I am taking you home."

That night Telu asked me, "What did you learn at school today?"
I learnt that a pig should not go to school.

books.title: About Birds

pages.text: What is different about birds? This eagle has wings that are long and wide. Are birds the only animals with wings?
No. Some insects have wings. This dragonfly has wings. Flying fish have fins that look like wings.
This parrot and hornbill have a bill. A bill can also be called a beak. Are birds the only animals with a bill?
No. A platypus has a bill.
Are birds the only animals that lay eggs?
No. Fish, frogs, snakes and turtles lay eggs.
The male bird of paradise has bright colours. Are birds the only animals with bright colours?
No. Beetles, ladybugs, butterflies and fish have bright colours.
This eagle and seagull have sharp eyes. Are birds the only animals with sharp eyes?
No. Many animals, such as cats and crocodiles, have sharp eyes.
This cassowary and owl have sharp claws. Are birds the only animals with sharp claws?
No. Cuscus, kangaroos and many other animals have sharp claws.
What makes birds different from other animals? Birds are the only animals with feathers.

Feathers are very useful.
• They keep the bird warm.
• They help the bird fly.
• Tail feathers help the bird to steer.
• The colour of their feathers helps birds to hide.
• The colour of their feathers also helps birds to find a mate.

“Shhhh...” said Aunty Jui, with her finger on her lips. “Softly. The baby is sleeping.”

Sleeping? What a bore. Anu began to sulk.

image.alt: Girl talking to a lady with a baby on her lap

pages.text:
Aai pulled Anu close. “The baby is still very small, Anu. You must not trouble her. After all, you are her big sister!”

Big sister! Anu felt very important. But why did the baby have to go to sleep?

image.alt: Lady holding girl close and talking to her

pages.text:
Just then they heard a thin wail...

“She is up,” said Aunty, and gave the baby to Aai.

“I want to hold the baby,” said Anu.

“Oh no, Anu. You won't be able to. You're much too small,” said Aai.

“But I'm her big sister,” said Anu.

image.alt: Girl and lady looking at a baby in another lady's lap

pages.text: Why should the baby sit on Aai's lap? I want to sit on Aai's lap too, thought Anu. But Aai said, “Anu, move away! You must not bother baby. See how tiny she is?”

image.alt: Lady holding a baby in her lap and speaking to a little girl

pages.text:
The baby was still wailing. “Waah...”

“Oh dear!” said Aunty. “I think she's soiled her nappy.”

She cleaned the baby and changed her nappy.

The baby gurgled happily.

image.alt: Two ladies changing a baby's nappy

pages.text:
Anu was disgusted. What a silly baby. Potty in the nappy!

And Aai and Aunty were mad! They didn't even scold the baby.

image.alt: Girl looking sulky

pages.text: If I just pee in my underwear by mistake, Aai glares at me. But now look at her doing ‘kootchie-coo!' to the baby! Wait till I get home. I'll tell Baba how unfair Aai is.

image.alt: Sulky girl

pages.text:
“Let's go home, Aai!” Anu cried.

“Why, Anu, don't you like the baby?” asked Aunty. “Chee!” said Anu.

“Silly baby, does potty in the nappy, doesn't talk, doesn't play. I don't like your baby. Why did you get yourself such a silly baby?”

image.alt: Girl talking to two ladies with a baby on one's lap

pages.text:
On the way back home, Anu asked her mother, “Aai, when will I become a baby?”

“You won't become a baby again, “ said Aai. “You'll grow bigger now.”

“I don't want to be big! I want to be a baby and I want to sleep in your lap, and I want to drink milk with a spoon and I want to sit on Baba's shoulders and go out and...”

Anu muttered all the way home.

image.alt: Girl and lady in saree talking

pages.text: The next day Aai said, ”Anu, let's give your small clothes, toys and cradle to Aunty Jui's baby, shall we?”

image.alt: Girl and lady looking at toys and clothes

pages.text:
“No!” yelled Anu. “That's my ball and my cradle!”

“Okay, what about giving away these clothes then? They're so small,” said Aai.

“No!” shouted Anu again. “I want to wear them, NOW!” So Aai put the small frock on Anu. She even put the little baby bonnet on her head.

image.alt: Girl holding a ball and wearing a frock and bonnet

pages.text:
Anu crawled all over the house.

She balanced the ball on her head and wandered around, calling, ‘Curd! Fresh curd!' She played with the rattle: rat-a-tat-tat.

image.alt: Girl wearing a frock, bonnet and playing with toys

pages.text:
Anu climbed into the cradle. She wanted to lie down and suck her thumb.

But she didn't fit! Her feet stuck out at one end, and she couldn't keep her arms straight. The tight little frock began to pinch. Anu was fed up. This was no fun at all!

image.alt: Girl sitting on cradle and sucking her thumb

pages.text:
Anu said to her mother, “Aai, why don't we give this frock and bonnet and cradle to Aunty Jui's baby?”

“Give it all away? But then what will you do?” asked Aai.

“Aai, I'm a big sister now, aren't I? Once you become a big sister you wear proper clothes, and sleep on the bed.”

“Oh really? I had no idea!” said Aai, smiling.

Anu wore her own clothes and said, “Aai, tell baby that her big sister has given her all this. You'll tell her, won't you?”

Anu jumped on to her scooter and went off to play.

image.alt: Girl on scootie talking to her mother

questions.q: Why did Anu get ready so fast?
What did Anu try to lie down in?
Why did Anu decide to give her baby things away?
choices: She felt proud to be a big sister

pages.text:
Bheema loves to sleep and just cannot get up early.

Ramu, the washerman, scolds Bheema often.

image.alt: Sleepy donkey

pages.text:
One day, Gauri, the cow, asked him, “Bheema, why are you so sad?”

Bheema said, “I cannot get up early and Ramu shouts at me every day. Will you wake me up every morning, please?”

“Yes, I will,” said Gauri. Early next morning, Gauri mooed loudly, but Bheema did not wake up.

image.alt: Cow looking at donkey sleeping

pages.text:
Coming back from the river in the evening, Bheema met Moti, the dog.

“I can never get up in the morning on time. Will you wake me up?” Bheema asked Moti.

“Yes, I will,” said Moti and the next morning he barked and barked but did Bheema wake up? No Sir!

image.alt: Donkey and dog

pages.text:
That evening Bheema met Cheenu, the rooster.

He said to Cheenu, “You crow in the morning and everybody wakes up. Will you wake me up too?”

Cheenu agreed. The next morning, Cheenu crowed long and loud, but Bheema did not wake up.

image.alt: Rooster crowing and donkey sleeping

pages.text:
The next evening, Bheema saw Kalu, the crow, cawing away happily.

“Kalu, will you wake me up in the morning, please?” he asked.

Kalu said, “Why not? I will caw and wake you up.”

The next morning Kalu cawed all he could but Bheema did not wake up.

image.alt: Crow sitting on donkey's back

pages.text:
Bheema was sad.

The next morning, a fly came and sat on his nose.

“Aaah...chhoooo... ahchhoo!” Bheema got up with a big sneeze.

image.alt: Fly on donkey's nose

pages.text:
“Wow! I woke up. How did I wake up?” he asked in wonder.

“I woke you up,” said the fly.“Will you wake me up like this early every morning?”

“Sure,” said the fly. Bheema was happy. Now he would have no problem getting up early every morning!

image.alt: Fly sitting on donkey's head

glossary.note: a person who washes clothes for other people

questions.q: Who scolds Bheema?
Who finally woke Bheema up?
Why did the fly's way of waking him work?

pages.text: School was about to get over. Just five minutes more, but Cheenu could not wait! He looked outside. There was nobody there. From somewhere close by, a bell jingled.

image.alt: Boy looking out of a classroom window

pages.text:
“Cheenu, what are you doing?” asked his teacher.

“Sorry Miss,” Cheenu said.

“It's just that...”

image.alt: Surprised boy

pages.text:
“Paperwala, kaidalu*! Papere kaidalu!” sang Cheenu's father, the Kabadiwala**. Even from outside, he could see Cheenu's grin.

*Kaidalu: Paper in Telugu, **Kabadiwala: Junk dealer in Hindi.

image.alt: A busy street

pages.text: The school bell rang. Cheenu ran out to his father, grinning from ear to ear. He was the only child in school whose father came to pick him up.

image.alt: Father picking up son from school

pages.text:
Cheenu jumped on to the bandi and dangled his legs. His father pushed the bandi*, shouting, “Paperwala... kaidalu!!!”

Cheenu also shouted. They were quite loud! When a watchman stopped them, Cheenu jumped off. He went with his father, carrying an empty sack. All the things they would get today would go into that sack.

*Bandi: Cart in Telugu.

image.alt: Push-cart on a busy street

pages.text:
From this house, newspapers.

From that one, newspapers and magazines.

From the ground floor, newspapers and magazines and empty bottles.

image.alt: Boy helping father carry newspapers

pages.text: Cheenu ran to the bandi to get another empty sack. They were going up in a lift! Cheenu's eyes grew big and round!

image.alt: Boy in an elevator

pages.text: From the fifth floor, newspapers and magazines, bottles and boxes and books.

image.alt: Boy playing with boxes and man packing

pages.text: While his father was talking to the lady, Cheenu put everything away so that the books were right on top. Where he could look at them!

image.alt: Man and woman in conversation while boy looks through the sack's contents

pages.text: This time, Cheenu had to help his father push the bandi!

image.alt: Boy helping man push the cart

pages.text:
At home, after they had put everything away, Cheenu's father called him. “I have something for you,” he said.

It was the book Cheenu had been looking at all afternoon!

“Thank you, Naana*!” Cheenu said. After that, they had to call him three times to come and have dinner!

*Naana: Father in Telugu.

image.alt: Boy reading as parents eat

glossary.note: a person who buys old newspapers, bottles and other things so they can be used again

questions.q: What does Cheenu's father do?
choices: He collects old paper and bottles

questions.q: How did Cheenu and his father get to the fifth floor?
Why did Cheenu's father give him the book?
choices: He saw how much Cheenu liked it

pages.text:
Nanhi picked up her slate and chalk.

She wanted to draw a long, l-o-n-g train.

image.alt: Girl carrying a slate and walking with dog

pages.text: Nanhi first drew an engine which gave out a lot of smoke, for the long, long train.

image.alt: Girl drawing on a slate and dog watching

pages.text: “Oh dear! Now where shall I make the coaches?” Nanhi wondered, for there was no more space on the slate.

image.alt: Girl holding slate and looking worried

pages.text: Nanhi put the slate and chalk down on the floor and thought.

image.alt: Girl and dog looking at slate

pages.text:
She drew a coach on the floor.

Then a second coach, then another, and another, and another... Nanhi just kept drawing.

image.alt: Drawing of a moving train

pages.text:
Until her chalk got over.

Nanhi got up and took a look. Wow!

Her train was as long as the verandah!

image.alt: Girl and dog watching a moving train

pages.text: And off went Nanhi's train – Chhuk-Chhuk-Chhak, from here to there, so very far!

image.alt: Girl and dog running happily with train in the background

glossary.note: a small board you write on with chalk

questions.q: What did Nanhi want to draw?
Where did Nanhi draw the coaches?
Why did Nanhi stop drawing on her slate?

books.title: Curious baby elephant

pages.text: Everyone knows that the elephant has a very long nose.
But a long time ago, the elephant’s nose was short and fat. Like a shoe in the middle of his face.
A curious baby elephant was born. She had a question for every animal.
She was curious about Giraffe. “Why do you have a long neck?” she asked.
She was curious about Rhino. “Why does your horn have a sharp point?”
She was curious about Hippo. “Why do you have red eyes?” she asked.
And she was VERY curious about Crocodile. “What does Crocodile eat for dinner?”
“Never ask a question like that!” said her mother. She walked off, frowning.
But clever Crow quickly said, “Follow me to the river. There you will see what Crocodile eats for dinner.”
So Baby Elephant followed Crow all the way down to the river.
She pushed through the reeds and stood on the bank. She looked into the water. Where was Crocodile?
“Hello,” said a stone near the river bank. “Hello,” said Baby Elephant. “Perhaps you can tell me what Crocodile eats for dinner?”

“Bend down and I will tell you,” said the stone. “Lower, lower...”
So Baby Elephant bent down lower, until…

“Snap!” Her nose was in the jaws of Crocodile.
“Crocodile will eat you for dinner!” squawked Crow.

Baby Elephant sat back on her strong legs and pulled, and pulled, and pulled.
But Crocodile did not let go.

Baby Elephant’s nose stretched, and stretched, and stretched, until…
“Duuffff!” she fell on her back.
Cross at losing his dinner, Crocodile slithered back into the water.

Baby Elephant looked at her nose.
She could not see where it ended!
It was so long she could pick fruit from high branches.
And shower herself with water on a hot day.
And to this day, all elephants have very long and useful trunks.

questions.q: What was the elephant's nose like long ago?
Who told Baby Elephant to follow him to the river?
How did Baby Elephant's nose become long?
choices: Crocodile pulled it and it stretched

pages.text:
Once upon a time there was a husband and wife with children.
The mother prepared food for the family each day. She would bring the meal to the table for them to eat.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_02_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
The father would divide the meat. He would say to the eldest child,
“I am old enough for meat. Here is yours. Wait until you are older.”

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_03_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
Then he would say to the next child, “I am old enough for meat. Here is yours. Wait until you are older.”
It went like this for all the children. The youngest child got the tiniest piece of meat.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_04_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
The father kept the big pieces of meat for himself and his wife.
The children were quiet and ate their food.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_05_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
Years passed and the children grew up. The parents grew old.
They became helpless.
The children took turns preparing food for their old mother and father.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_06_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text: One day at meal time, the eldest child served the meat as usual. But this time she gave only a tiny piece to her father and a tiny piece to her mother.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_07_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
She said to her parents, “You ate yours, now it is our time.
We are old enough.”
She served most of the meat to her brothers and sisters.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_08_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
The father remembered what he did while his children were young.
Mother and father agreed that it was not the right thing to do.
They asked for forgiveness.
The children promised that they would not repeat this mistake with their own children.

image.alt: This picture, ASP_148_elders_0_Page_09_Image_0001.png, is missing or was loading too slowly.

questions.q: Who kept the big pieces of meat when the children were young?
Who served the meat when the parents grew old?
What did the parents learn?
choices: Their way of sharing was not fair

pages.text:
It was a bright moonlit night. All the animals in Mangu's farm were sleeping.

Except Tinku!

image.alt: Farm animals sleeping at night

pages.text:
“I am not sleepy, Ma,” murmured Tinku. But Ma did not hear him. She was fast asleep.

He turned left, and he turned right. He lay on his tummy, and rolled on his back. But he could not sleep!

image.alt: Dog awake at night

pages.text:
So he set off into the night to see what he could find. Up in the sky, Tinku saw the moon, white and round, smiling down at him. He felt very happy.

‘Night is beautiful,' thought Tinku.

image.alt: Dog running out of farm at night

pages.text:
Far away on the top of a tree, there were some tiny lights. One spot of light flew down! “I'm a firefly,” said the spot of light. “I glow in the dark!”

“Will you be my friend?” asked Tinku.

“Yes, I will!” said the firefly.

image.alt: Dog talking to firefly at night

pages.text:
Something flew by and hung upside down on a tree.

“What is your name, bird?” asked Tinku.

“I am not a bird, I am a bat. I can see during the night!” said the bat.

“Will you be my friend?” asked Tinku.

“Yes, I will!” said the bat.

image.alt: Dog talking to bat at night

pages.text:
A few leaves moved in the bushes. Someone was hiding! “Who are you?” asked Tinku.

“I am a fox,” said the fox. “I go strolling out at night.”

“Will you be my friend?” asked Tinku.

“Yes, I will!” said the fox.

image.alt: Dog talking to fox at night

pages.text:
Two shiny eyes looked at him from a tree. “Who are you?” asked Tinku.

“I'm an owl,” said the owl. “I hunt for food during the night.”

“Will you be my friend?” asked Tinku.

“Yes, I will!” said the owl.

image.alt: Dog talking to owl at night

pages.text:
“CHIRRRRRP! CHIRRRRRP!”

“Who is here?” Tinku asked.

“I'm a cricket,” said the cricket. “I chirp when it is dark.”

“Will you be my friend?” asked Tinku.

“Yes, I will!” said the cricket.

image.alt: Dog talking to cricket at night

pages.text:
Tinku and his friends jumped and tossed and rolled until Tinku yawned. “I am sleepy. I have to go home now,” said Tinku. He was happy that he had many new friends.

Snuggling close to Ma, he said, “Night is not a lonely place, Ma. Night is full of wonderful beings.”

“Yes!” replied Ma. “Your new friends are nocturnal, just like wild dogs.”

image.alt: Dog, firefly, bat, fox, owl and cricket

pages.text: “Nocturnal animals eat, play and work at night. They rest during the day. You must sleep now. Sleep will give you energy to play with your day-time friends tomorrow. Good night, little one!” she said, hugging him tight.

image.alt: Dog hugging puppy at night

pages.text:
The bright round moon shone all night long, spreading her calm light all around.

And Tinku slept all through the night!

image.alt: Dog and puppy sleeping at night

questions.q: Why did Tinku go out into the night?
Which new friend glows in the dark?
Ma says Tinku's new friends are nocturnal. What does that mean?

pages.text:
Nani keeps losing her glasses.

“Where did I keep them?” she always asks. Without her glasses, she cannot find her glasses.

image.alt: Girl standing on the cot, Lady standing

pages.text: So she needs me. To be her eyes, to find her own eyes!

image.alt: Girl standing on a bed

pages.text:
Sometimes her spectacles are in the bathroom. Or on her bed. Or on her head.

“Nani,” I say, “they are on your head!”

image.alt: Girl behind a cot, Lady knitting

pages.text:
“Of course! How silly of me. Thank you, Richa dear,” she says with a giggle.

This time, though, I cannot find Nani's glasses. Not yet.

image.alt: Girl crouching behind a bed and watching her grandmother knit

pages.text:
I have looked everywhere. In all the usual places. On her head, in the bathroom, inside her cupboard, and on the puja shelf. I have looked under her favourite chair and on the dining table.

Nothing. No glasses. Where could they be?

image.alt: Girl under a chair, Open Cupboard

pages.text: I decided to be a good detective. I decided to find out what she had done all day.

image.alt: Women eating and drinking at the dining table, with girl standing

pages.text: “I did nothing much today. Except that Veena's mother-in-law came, you know. And how much she gossips! We had many cups of tea. And she ate all the laddoos your mother had made,” said Nani.

image.alt: Women drinking tea and having snacks at the table

pages.text: Raju said, “Nani was very busy today. She wrote a letter to the Chief Minister about her pension.”

image.alt: Woman and girl holding a sweater, Cat following a girl, lady writing a letter

pages.text:
Amma said, “She spoke for a long time to your Masi. She finished knitting the sweater for Raju. And then she went for a short walk.”

I now had many clues. I quickly looked around new places in the house.

Aha! I have found the missing glasses!

image.alt: Letter being written, Old woman and girl holding an orange sweater

pages.text:
The spectacles were wrapped in wool, kept next to her pen, under the phone, on her desk. And I found a half-eaten laddoo there as well. For Nani's next birthday, I will save money for an extra pair of glasses!

Nani: Hindi word for grandmother

Masi: Hindi word for mother's sister

image.alt: Girl looking at Telephone and Spectacles

questions.q: Where are Nani's glasses sometimes?
Where were the glasses this time?
choices: Wrapped in wool on her desk

questions.q: How did Richa find the glasses?
choices: She found out what Nani did all day, like a detective

pages.text:
A long time ago, in the village of Nyamani, there lived a man known as Kiundu.
He liked to eat meat a lot.
One day, the chief of Nyamani village invited all the villagers to his son’s wedding.

Kiundu also heard that there was another wedding party in Katumbi village.
“Ugh! Two parties on the same day!” Kiundu thought.
“I must attend both parties,” Kiundu said. “I will first walk to Katumbi then come back to Nyamani.”

Kiundu woke up early in the morning and walked to Katumbi village. He looked around and saw that the party had not yet started. “I will go back to Nyamani and return to Katumbi later,” Kiundu decided.
Kiundu walked back to Nyamani hoping to find the meat ready. He was now very hungry. When he arrived, people were still preparing the food.
“I left cooks at Katumbi preparing to cook,” he thought. “The food must be ready now.” Kiundu decided to go back to Katumbi.

When Kiundu arrived at the Katumbi party, people had already eaten. Guests were giving presents to the bride and the groom. Kiundu was very mean. He did not have a present to give. He only wanted to eat.
Kiundu was very disappointed about missing the food. He decided to walk back to Nyamani village. Because he was hungry and tired, he could not walk fast.
When he arrived at Nyamani village, people were singing and dancing. They had already eaten all the food.
Upon hearing that there was no food, Kiundu fainted. He had missed meat from both parties. When he recovered, he got some porridge in a small cup!
Slowly, he walked home sad and hungry.

questions.q: What did Kiundu like to eat?
How many parties were on the same day?
Why did Kiundu miss the food at both parties?
choices: He kept walking back and forth

pages.text:
One morning Greeny the dinosaur decided to go on a little adventure. "Bye Mom! I will be back in the afternoon! I am going to sail down the river to explore," he said.
His mom replied, "Make sure to pack some lunch and stay safe! Have fun!" So Greeny set off in his little red boat down the river.

"Here is a nice spot to stop. I will pick some flowers for Mom first," said Greeny. As he was about to pick a nice purple flower he saw a small grasshopper sitting on a leaf. "Hello! My name is Greeny," Greeny said, "What is your name?"
"I am Hoppers. Let's be friends!" replied the grasshopper.
"Ok!" replied Greeny.

The two friends decided that they would spend the entire day together. "The day is so nice. It makes me want to dance!!" exclaimed Hoppers.
"Let's dance together!" replied Greeny.
The two then pranced around the flower fields until they were too tired to move.

"Thanks for playing with me today Hoppers! I had so much fun! But Mom is waiting for me at home. I have to go back now," said Greeny.
"I had so much fun today too! Maybe we can meet sometime next week! Bye until next time!" replied Hoppers.

questions.q: How does Greeny travel down the river?
What kind of animal is Hoppers?
Why does Greeny have to go home?
choices: His mom is waiting for him

pages.text:
“What's wrong Grandpa, why are you not reading the newspaper?”

asked Gulli one morning.

“Oh dear, I broke my reading glasses, and I can't read anything without them,”said Grandpa.

image.alt: A boy and an old man with a newspaper in his hand

pages.text:
“Ah, don't you worry, Grandpa. Let me go and get my box of things.”

Gulli ran out fast, and came back with his little brown box.

image.alt: Boy running and carrying a box

pages.text:
Clink, clonk, dadum-dum. What has he found at last?

A shining bright magnifying glass!

If you care to look through it, everything will look better and bigger.

image.alt: Boy using a magnifying glass

pages.text: "Thank you, this is just fine, now I can read each and every line," said Grandpa.

image.alt: Boy and an old man using a magnifying glass to read

pages.text:
“What is wrong, Mangal Chacha?” asked Gulli one Sunday.

“I have to pour oil from this pack, but the bottle's neck is so small. I am sure I will make a complete mess in my kitchen,” said Mangal Chacha.

“Ah, don't worry, let me find you something really fast,” said Gulli.

image.alt: Boy and man in the kitchen

pages.text: Clink, clonk, dadum-dum, let's see what Gulli has found this time!

image.alt: Boy sifting through a box

pages.text:
A funnel with a big, wide mouth! Pour anything from the top, and see how it comes down so neatly, drop by drop!

"Here, Mangal Chacha, use this one, the kitchen will be clean and cooking will be fun."

image.alt: Boy holding a funnel and dancing

pages.text: "Thank you Gulli, for helping me out!"

image.alt: Boy eating and man pouring oil in a kitchen

pages.text:
“What are you looking for, Grandma?” asked Gulli.

“Oh, I was mending Grandpa's monkey cap, and the needle just fell off from my lap!” said Grandma.

“You just sit here on the chair that rocks, while I go find something from my little brown box!” said Gulli.

image.alt: Boy with a cricket bat and old woman

pages.text:
Clink, clonk, dadum-dum, what has Gulli found this time?

A magnet! All the little metal things will stick to that!

"Let me scan the ground, and the needle will soon be found," said Gulli.

image.alt: Boy using a magnet

pages.text:
“Look Grandma, see how your needle is stuck, and I also found other long-lost metal stuff!”

“Thank you Gulli, you are so wise. Your little brown box is really nice!” said Grandma.

image.alt: Boy holding a magnet and running towards old woman

glossary.note: uncle (a father's younger brother) in Hindi

questions.q: Why can't Grandpa read the newspaper?
What does Gulli give Mangal Chacha to pour the oil?
What kind of boy is Gulli?

pages.text:
Hippo wants to dance. She jumps up and down on the dusty ground.
Thump! Thump!
“You’re getting dirt on me!” says Shongololo, sleeping in the sand. “Go dance somewhere else.”

Hippo wants to dance. She rolls into the river and splashes her arms and legs.
Splish! Splash!
“You’re making me wet!” says Kingfisher, hunting for her breakfast. “Go dance somewhere else.”

Hippo wants to dance. She twirls around and around in a field, kicking her legs up high.
Swoosh! Swoosh!
“Be careful! You nearly kicked me!” says Meerkat, bathing his babies. “Go dance somewhere else.”

Hippo wants to dance. She flops into a puddle of mud and slides around on her nice big belly.
Squish! Squash!
“Why don’t you stop dancing?” asks Donkey, carrying his buckets. “Why can’t you do something useful instead?”
Hippo is sad. She is too sad to dance. She sits on a rock and cries. The tears roll down her cheeks and fall on the ground.

Plop! Plop!
Grasshopper hears Hippo’s tears. He starts dancing around her feet.
Hop! Hop!
Hippo and Grasshopper start to dance, and the other animals come to look …

questions.q: Who is sleeping in the sand?
Why is Hippo sad?
choices: Everyone tells her to stop dancing

questions.q: Who starts dancing around Hippo's feet?

books.title: How Ant Saved Dove

pages.text: It was a hot summer day in the dry forest.
Little Ant had not drunk water for many days.
"I need a drop of water, even if it falls from a leaf," cried Little Ant.
But even the dew on the leaves had dried up.

"If I do not have water, I will die," cried Little Ant.
"I must find the river."

"The river is full and strong.
It will sweep you away," warned a wise squirrel.

But Little Ant was extremely thirsty.
I will die if I don't drink some water, he thought.
So, he went to look for the river.
He walked past tufts of grass, and he climbed over dry branches.

He walked until he heard the sound of water splashing.
It was the river!
He could hear the slosh of the waves.
At the edge of the river, Little Ant took a long sip of cool water.
He was so happy he did not see a wave coming.

The wave crashed over Little Ant.
He tried to grab some grass floating past him.
But he was swept away by the water.
"Help me someone! Help me please!" he called.
"Quick, climb on," said White Dove, holding a branch in her beak.
White Dove lifted Little Ant to safety, and then she flew away.

"I will stay here until I can thank the dove," decided Little Ant.
"I will wait until she comes back to drink."

One day as he waited, two boys came to the river.
They had their slingshots.

"There is a big, white dove that comes here to drink," said one boy.
"We will have it for supper tonight."

"I cannot let the boys kill White Dove," thought Little Ant.
"But I am so tiny, what can I do?"
Just then White Dove flew down from the tree to drink.
Little Ant had an idea.

He jumped onto one boy's foot.
Little Ant bit the boy as hard as he could.
The boy jumped. "Ouch!" he shouted.
White Dove was startled and flew away to safety.
That was how Little Ant thanked White Dove for saving his life.

pages.text: Once long ago, the birds had a meeting. They wanted a king, just like people and animals. Which bird should be king?

pages.text:
"I think I should be king," said Peacock, fanning his tail. "I am so beautiful."

"You are too proud," said Owl. "I have the largest eyes of any bird. I should be king." "No, not you, Owl," they shouted. "You go to sleep when the sun rises."

image.alt: Dancing peacock and owl

pages.text:

“Yes, yes,” they shouted, and they all flew up, up, into the sky.

pages.text: Mother was finishing packing her clothes in a small bag.
As she went out the door, she hugged me and said, “Bye for now.”
“Where are you going, mum?” I looked up at her as I asked.
I started to cry, wanting to follow her but dad lifted me up on his shoulder.
Dad said, “Your mother is going to the hospital to have a baby.”
When I heard “baby” I stopped crying and looked at him. “Why is she going to get the baby from the hospital?” I asked him.

Dad sat me on a small chair and said, “I will tell you why she is going to get the baby from the hospital.”
I listened keenly to him as he explained although I didn’t quite understand why she wasn’t having the baby at home.

When dad finished explaining, I asked, “Will she still love me when she comes back with the other baby?”
My dad held me close and said, “We will always love you.”
“Can I write a letter to her while she is there?” I asked dad.
That evening, I began to write a letter to mum.
I tore a paper from my exercise book and began to write…
“Mummy, mummy, dad said that you have gone to bring another baby…
…Please hurry up and return home…
…I want you to bring a baby girl, so I can play with her when she grows up…
…I am waiting for you here outside our house.”
I folded my letter so I could give it to my father to bring it to mum. When I woke up the following morning, the letter was gone.

pages.text: One night Grandpa was tucking me in. His hands were soft and his hair was thin.
‘I’m going to tell you a special story, about a girl named Lory Dory.’
You couldn’t see Lory Dory at all because she was born invisible.
You’d only see Lory when rain hit her head, or when she was curled under blankets in bed.
‘Look, it’s Lory. The Imaginary Friend! She’s not like us, she’s just pretend!’
One day at school, a boy wanted to know: ‘How do you look? I only see you in snow.’
‘Can you paint yourself?’ Lory knew that she could.
Lory painted her body with all that she loved from the world all around and the sky up above.
She painted herself every day with such pride, to bring out the person who she was inside.
‘I know I’m invisible and hard to see. So I painted these pictures to show the real me.’

‘Are you making this up, Gramps? Is this story true?’
‘Lory is real – real as me, real as you.’
When Grandpa had left me, I can’t quite be sure, but I think I saw Lory just outside my door.

My brother Mannu and I go to the balwadi.

It is a small school for little children like us.

We leave our shoes and slippers by the door.

Everyone puts their shoes or slippers in a line.

It looks good that way.

Some boxes are big. Others are small.

Water bottles are hung on the wall.

The bottles are of different colours. Red, blue, green, yellow.

I like to count. Mannu plays with blocks and puts different shapes together. He likes to play with beads. I like the cards with dots.

Our teacher says playing with these toys is good for the brain.

We read books. Some books have pictures.

The teacher helps us to learn the letters. She says I will read soon because I can recognize all the letters. I can also read sentences.

She does not know it.

Now it is time for stories. Our teacher has puppets.

The teacher uses the puppets to tell us stories.

The puppets speak in a funny voice.

My friends think that the puppets can speak. They are surprised.

But I am not. Puppets do not talk.

I know that it is the teacher who speaks in a funny voice for them.

It is now time to play. The school has a tub with some play dough. Mannu likes to make shapes out of the dough. I like to make fruits, toys and other things.

pages.text: It was a hot summer afternoon.
Lilato fanned herself.

“If only it could rain,” her brother, Mayamiko, said.
It was too hot to let the children play outside.

Ndo-ndo!
Lilato heard it first. It sounded like a stone bouncing on the roof of the house. Lilato looked at Mayamiko but he didn’t look at her.
She tiptoed to the window and looked up at the sky. The sky was grey, almost black in colour.

Lilato started to sing the song her best friend, Mwansa, had taught her.
Wemfula isa isa
O rain come
Twangale na mainsa
So we can play in the rain
Wemfula isa isa
O rain come
Twangale na mainsa
So we can play in the rain
Lilato sang, rubbing her fingers together.

Ndo-ndo-ndo-ndo-ndo-ndo!
More raindrops fell from the sky.
“Maya! It’s raining!” Lilato yelled. “It’s raining!” They ran outside the house.
Mama was already putting buckets around the house to collect rainwater.
They ran to the road in front of their house and joined other children.

A chorus of wemfula isa isa twangale na mainsa, was heard all over the neighbourhood.
The sky opened and poured more rain, joining into the music of the day.

books.title: Oh the Way We Ran, in the Fish Rain

pages.text:
Dark clouds gathered over the hills as Akira was leaving home on a windy day.

"Don't forget to get our umbrella from Gopu's shop. It looks like it's going to rain," said Akira's father. But just as Akira and Zero - her pet cat - started to walk towards the rusty old bridge, it began to rain...

image.alt: Father saying bye to daughter

pages.text:
... FISH!

An endless stream of fish was falling from the sky.

Thin fish, fat fish, blue fish, golden fish, upside down fish, slanting fish - oh, hundreds and hundreds of falling fish!

But Akira couldn't be late. So they ran and ran, in the fish rain.

image.alt: Girl and cat running over a bridge, fish rain

pages.text:
Across Kabir's fields they sprang, with the wind howling in their ears and a strong fishy smell tickling their noses.

But they couldn't be late. So they ran and ran, in the fish rain...

image.alt: Girl and cat running through fish rain

pages.text:
Until Akira noticed that Zero was no longer with her. But it wasn't hard to find him.

"Stay with me, Zero. You know I can't be late today," she said.

So they ran and ran, in the fish rain.

image.alt: Falling fish, girl watching cat eat fish

pages.text:
Soon they reached the market street. People were holding their baskets high to catch as many falling fish as possible. "Fish for sale! Fresh, fresh fish for sale!" The market was already filled with their loud, excited cries, and it made Akira and Zero feel just a little hungry.

But they couldn't be late. So they ran and ran, in the fish rain...

image.alt: Market place

pages.text:
Until, all of a sudden, fish stopped falling from the sky.

Slowly, the clouds parted, and there it was - a grand, smiling rainbow.

Akira jumped with joy and reached out to the sky.

They had reached school just in time. And finally, no more running in the fish rain!

image.alt: Girl under a rainbow

questions.q: What fell from the sky instead of rain?
What were the people at the market doing?
choices: Holding up baskets to catch the fish

questions.q: Why did Akira keep running all the way?
choices: She was scared of the fish
She did not want to be late for school

pages.text: Pehelwaan ji exercised every day.

image.alt: Man exercising

pages.text:
One day, he wanted to be a player. He went to the field and said to the children, “I want to play with you.”

The children were scared of him. So they could not say no to him!

image.alt: Man speaking to a group of children

pages.text: When Pehelwaan kicked the ball it almost burst. When he kicked it again, the goalkeeper went flying!

image.alt: Ball and boy flying in the air

pages.text: The children did not know what to do.

image.alt: Smiling man, worried boys

pages.text:
Gappu said, “Pehelwaan ji, let us play cricket.”

Pehelwaan ji said, “Yes, but I will bat first.”

image.alt: Man speaking to a boy holding a cricket bat

pages.text: Gappu ran, and jumped high as he threw the ball.

image.alt: Boy throwing something

pages.text: Pehelwaan ji lifted the bat. He lost his balance. The ball hit his head. Ouch!

image.alt: Man hit by a ball

pages.text:
Pehelwaan said, “Now, I will bowl.”

Gappu said, “Fine Pehelwaan ji, but please do not jump high when you bowl. That will scare me.”

image.alt: Man getting ready to bowl while playing cricket with a boy

pages.text: Pehelwaan did not listen to Gappu. He jumped high.

image.alt: Man throwing a ball

pages.text: He lost his balance and fell down. THUD!

image.alt: Man falling down

pages.text:
He got up and said, "I will field now."

Gappu nodded his head.

image.alt: Bruised man and boy with a cricket bat

pages.text: Gappu turned his bat this way and that. The ball went all over the field. Zipp, zapp, zipp, zoom. Pehelwaan ji huffed and puffed as he ran after it. OHH, AAAH, HMMPH.

image.alt: Man running as boy bats

pages.text:
Pehelwaan ji was very tired.

He pulled a face and said, “This is not for me! I will be the wicket-keeper.” Gappu agreed.

image.alt: Injured man speaking to boy with cricket bat

pages.text: Gappu threw the ball up high. The batsman ducked. Pehelwaan ji could do nothing as the ball went straight into his mouth... GUPP!

image.alt: Boy with cricket bat, man with ball inside his mouth

pages.text:
“Forget it. I don't want to play!” said Pehelwaan ji.

He was in bad shape as he ran away. Gappu pulled out a new ball and everybody went back to the game peacefully.

pages.text:
Phani is always late. Or not where he is supposed to be.

“Why does your teacher say you're always late for school, Phani?” asks his father. “You leave home quite early.”

“I can't help it, Baba,” Phani says.

image.alt: Angry man and woman scolding a boy

pages.text:
His mother wants to know why he is sitting in front of the TV every evening instead of playing with the other children.

“I can't help it, Ma,” says Phani.

image.alt: Angry woman scolding a boy who is watching TV

pages.text: Why not, his parents want to know. So do his teachers, friends and his sister, who had once asked him to post a letter.

image.alt: Worried family

pages.text:
“Why can't you help it, Phani?” they ask.

“It's because of my chappals,” Phani mumbles.

image.alt: Boy wearing his slippers

pages.text:
“Speak up, child! Stand up straight, shoulders back!”

That was his class teacher.

image.alt: Boy in class being scolded by teacher

pages.text: So Phani explains. Every time he is on his way to school, his chappals know a better way to get there. Sometimes, they lead by the mango tree where there are lovely green mangoes.

image.alt: Boy explaining and man imagining the explanation

pages.text: Sometimes, when his feet are sweating all over the chappals, they take him to school by a road that just happens to be near a clear, cool pond.

image.alt: Boy at the pond

pages.text:
And the chappals prefer to watch TV than be hurled at a pile of seven stones. Anybody should know that!

“Next time your chappals don't feel like posting a letter, at least let me know!” says Phani's sister angrily.

image.alt: Boy and girl talking

pages.text:
Nobody believes Phani.

Today, Phani's mother has something for him. Phani is very happy.

image.alt: Boy opening a box at home, surrounded by family

pages.text: He opens the box and takes out a new pair of chappals!

image.alt: Boy opening a new pair of chappals

pages.text: His mother is smiling...

image.alt: Sulking boy being watched by a woman and a girl

pages.text: But Phani doesn't look very happy. I wonder why!

image.alt: Boy leaving home for school

pages.text:
Once upon a time there was a little girl called Ramya. Ramya loved earrings. Everybody who gave her gifts, gave her earrings. She had red earrings, blue earrings, green earrings, and earrings of all the colours in the rainbow.

Then, for Ramya's birthday, do you know what her Grandma got her?

image.alt: Girl and rainbow

pages.text: Grandma got Ramya really pretty diamond earrings that looked like stars! Ramya loved them. "Oh! Grandma, from where did you get such pretty diamond stars?" she asked.

image.alt: Star earrings

pages.text: It was a starless night, and Grandma pointed to the sky. "See, there are no stars in the sky any longer. I plucked all the stars from the sky and chose the best ones for your earrings," Grandma replied.

image.alt: Night sky and full moon

pages.text:
This made Ramya very sad.

"Twinkle, twinkle little star,

How I wonder where you are?

Up above the world so high,

Please come back like diamonds in the sky!"

Ramya sang unhappily.

image.alt: Girl looking at moon from window

pages.text:
That night, Ramya took off her earrings and placed them carefully under her pillow. She hoped a fairy would return the stars to the sky.

In the middle of the night, Ramya had a beautiful dream.

image.alt: Girl sleeping in a bedroom

pages.text:
In the dream, a pretty fairy came and told Ramya, “Don't worry Ramya, I have thousands of new stars for the sky!”

Ramya woke up, and do you know what she saw?

image.alt: Fairy at night

pages.text: The night sky was filled with stars!

image.alt: Girl with teddy bear under the night-sky

pages.text: Ramya's eyes sparkled as she put on her precious diamond star earrings again!

image.alt: Smiling girl with sparkling eyes

pages.text: Now, Ramya is so happy!

image.alt: Night sky through a window

questions.q: What did Ramya love?
Where did Ramya put her earrings that night?
Why did Ramya feel sad?
choices: She thought the sky had no stars because of her earrings

pages.text:
Grandpa was writing a letter. Ritu stood beside him, leaning on the arm of the old chair.

“Grandpa, have you asked Aunty to send Mani to our home for the holidays?”

image.alt: Girl talking to grandfather

pages.text: “Of course, dear Ritu, I have written to your Aunty. Look here, let me read out the letter - Dear Pooja, Hope you are fine. Mani must be having holidays now. Ritu is very eager to see him. Do send him here to Tumkur.”

image.alt: Grandfather, girl and dog

pages.text:
Ritu jumped up and down. And since she could not stop herself, she ran around the room once and hugged Grandpa.

“Would you like to post this letter yourself?” asked Grandpa.

Ritu's eyes opened wide. “All by myself? Oh, may I?”

image.alt: Girl hugging man

pages.text:
“Yes, little Ritu. See, I have written the address. Take it to the Post Office. Give the postcard to Ramesh Uncle. You do know that big uncle with the big, handle-bar moustaches, don't you?”

“Yes Grandpa. He is the uncle who taught Mani how to ride the cycle last summer. Will he take the letter to Aunty Pooja?” asked Ritu.

“No, dear. But the letter will reach your aunty, don't worry.”

image.alt: Man helping boy cycle

pages.text:
Ritu picked up her little pink bag. She put the postcard inside. She put a pencil inside too. She felt very important.

Ritu felt very grown-up. And just a wee bit scared: what if Bageera the dog chased her?

But Ritu was very eager to post the letter. So she left for the post office that was just four buildings away!

image.alt: Girl running from dog

pages.text:
After taking a few steps,

Ritu stopped and took out the letter. She could not read Grandpa's handwriting very well. She tried to remember what Grandpa had read.

Then, after the word that she thought was ‘Tumkur' Ritu wrote, ‘PLEECE.' Happy with her work, Ritu walked on.

image.alt: Girl writing a letter and dog watching

pages.text: After she had reached the next building, Ritu stopped and took out the postcard once again. What if Pooja Aunty did not realise how eager Ritu was to see Mani? So Ritu took out her pencil again and wrote, ‘PLEEEESE.'

image.alt: Girl writing letter with a dog by her side

pages.text: Finally, Ritu reached the small post office. There was a red post box outside the post office. Ritu could not reach the mouth of the post box even if she stood on her toes.

image.alt: Girl posting a letter at post office

pages.text:
She walked boldly up to Uncle Ramesh. He took the postcard from her and smiled. “Smart girl! Now run back to your house carefully. I shall make sure your letter reaches your aunty.”

But Ritu did not run out. She saw Uncle Ramesh pick up a pen and scribble something on the card. Then he gave it to the postman who was stamping many letters with the postmark.

image.alt: Postman holding letter

pages.text: Dhhum, dhhum, DHHUM, he pounded on the letters. When he saw Ritu's letter, he stopped. Then he smiled. He picked out a pencil from behind his ear and wrote something on the card.

image.alt: Girl and dog with postman

pages.text:
Five days passed. The postman brought a letter to Grandpa. Grandpa read it with a smile. “Ritu, your aunty says she will send Mani here day-after. Let me read out the letter.

Dear Father...

tara...ra...ra...da...

ta...da...da...dada...

I am sending Mani tomorrow. He will reach Tumkur on Friday. I think Ritu must be very eager to see him. Your letter was very interesting...”

image.alt: Girl, man, postman and dog

pages.text:
“Grandpa, I wrote ‘PLEECE' on the letter, that's why!” said Ritu in excitement.

“.... Your postcard had twenty ‘Please's written all over it!”

image.alt: Happy girl jumping

pages.text:
Ritu did not know how one ‘please' had become twenty.

She was just happy she had added one ‘PLEECE' And another ‘PLEEEESE!'

image.alt: Man and playful dog

pages.text:
Pleese Pleece

PLEASE PLIS pleej

pleece Please

pleej PLIS pleece

PLEASE Pleeese PLEASE

image.alt: People laughing at letter

What word did Ritu add to the letter?
Why did the letter end up with so many "please"s?
choices: The people at the post office added more

One afternoon, Saboo was playing alone in the garden “Mother can I have a small puppy?”

“No,” said mother.

“A very small puppy?”

asked Saboo.

“No,” said mother.

pages.text: Saboo kicked a stone, which rolled near a tree. The tree trunk had fur. He touched it and looked up, up, and right up. He saw two eyes looking down at him.

image.alt: Boy touching a giraffe's legs

pages.text:
“Hello! Who are you?” asked a surprised Saboo.

“Hello yourself, I am a giraffe. My name is Jojo. I can play with you. If you climb up on to my back, I will take you for a ride.”

image.alt: Giraffe and boy looking at each other

pages.text:
Saboo climbed up and away they went down the road, up the hill, and into town.

Saboo shouted happily,

“Jojo turn right, now left, and again right,” till they came to his friend Munni's house.

image.alt: Boy sitting on giraffe's beck

pages.text: It was Munni's birthday. The children clapped when they saw Saboo on Jojo's back. Jojo helped Aunty put up the balloons. He was soooo...o tall, it was easy for him.

image.alt: A giraffe at a children's party

pages.text:
Jojo gave the children rides, he even played kick ball with them. It was a fun party.

Everyone sang, “Happy birthday to you.” Aunty put samosas, gulab jamuns, and ice-creams on the table.

image.alt: Happy boy on top of a giraffe

pages.text:
Jojo loved the ice-cream, so uncle got him a bucketful of ice-cream. Jojo finished it all. It was time to go home.

They said, “Bye Jojo, bye Saboo.”

Saboo and Jojo made their way back home. Mother was standing at the gate.

image.alt: Young boy clinging to a giraffe's neck

pages.text:
When she saw Saboo riding a giraffe, she was so... so... shocked.

“Saboo... I... said,”

“Mother you said, no small puppy, you did not say, no big tall giraffe.” Before mother could answer, the zookeeper came and took Jojo back to the zoo.

image.alt: Worried woman and smiling boy at the gate

Sara has a canoe.
Her canoe is big.
It is by the riverside.

Some women come to the river.
One woman has a basin of fruit.
Another woman has a chicken.
Another woman has a goat.
Another woman has two goats.
They ask Sara, “How can we get to the other side of the river?”
Sara says, “Get in my canoe!”

Then, some men arrive.
One man has a fish.
Another man has a bicycle.
Another man has a sack of maize.
Another man has two sacks of maize.

They ask Sara, “How can we get to the other side of the river?”
Sara replies, “Get in my canoe!”

Some animals come to the river.
They ask Sara, “How can we get across the river?”
Sara says, “Get in my canoe!”

The animals get in the canoe.
The dog gets in the canoe.
The cat gets in the canoe.
The monkey gets in the canoe.
The rabbit gets in the canoe.
The turtle gets in the canoe.
The gazelle gets in the canoe.

The elephant arrives at the river.
He asks, “How can I get to the other side of the river?”
Sara says, “Get in my canoe!”
The elephant gets in the canoe.

The canoe is too small.
There isn’t enough room.
The canoe fills up with water.
Sara says, “Hold on! First I’ll take the women.”
“Second, I’ll take the men.”
“Finally, I’ll take the animals.”
Elephant says, “Hey, I’ll walk!”

books.title: Satya, Watch Out!

pages.text:
Satya can’t stay still.
He runs and jumps and spins and rolls...
... and falls!

"Sit quietly for a minute!" says Appa.
"If you get hurt, don’t come crying to me," says Akka.

"Don’t you dare break anything!" says Thaatha.
"You're disturbing the class," says his teacher.
But what can Satya do if his hands and legs are always dancing?

Today is Sunday.
It’s Satya’s favourite day of the week — the day he goes to the farm where Amma works.
It’s a long walk to the farm, through secret up-and-down paths, open fields, thick forests and gently flowing streams.

Satya hops like a hare and sprints like a deer.
"The mud is squishy. Be careful!" says Amma.

He crawls like a centipede and slithers like a snake.
"Look out for thorns!" says Amma.

He swings like a spider and leaps like a langur.
"Wheeeee!"
"Use the strong branches, my little monkey," says Amma.

He paddles like a duck and swims like a frog.
“Stay in the shallows, okay?” says Amma.

He climbs like a lizard and jumps like a goat.
"Don’t slip!" says Amma.

Satya flaps his arms like wings and tries to fly away.
He imagines himself soaring and gliding like a vulture.

Late in the evening, when the sun sets and crickets begin to hum, it’s time to go home.
Tired Satya climbs on to his mother's back. They return through the up-and-down paths, fields, forests and streams.
At home, Appa, Akka and Thaatha take one look at bruised and muddy Satya, and burst into laughter.

Thaatha bathes him.
Appa cooks him dinner.
Akka tells him his favourite story as he falls asleep.
In his dreams, Satya runs and jumps and spins and rolls...
... and flies away!

pages.text: One day at school Sipho was trying very hard to read the book his teacher had given him. He tried and tried, but he couldn’t understand the story.
Sipho’s friend, Thembi, came over and grabbed the book from him. “It’s break time, Sipho! You’re still sitting here?”

Sipho looked sadly at Thembi and said, “Hey, Thembi! Miss Noah said we must read this, but I don’t really understand the story. It’s too hard.”
Thembi felt bad for her friend.

She searched for something in her bag, and took out a small book for Sipho.
They sat down to read the book together.

Sipho exclaimed, “Chicken is a sore loser!”
They laughed and chatted about the story.

“This story makes sense when we read it,” he said happily. Sipho finally enjoyed reading because the book was written in his language—isiXhosa!
“Thembi,” said Sipho, “where did you get this book? I also want a book like this.”

Thembi smiled and gave him the little book. “I go to a reading club on Saturdays. Would you like to come with me?”
“Let me show my mom this book and I’ll ask if I can join you,” he said.

Sipho read the book to his mom as soon as he got home.
His mom loved the book. She was happy to see him excited about reading at last!

When Thembi and Sipho arrived at the reading club, the place was full of children. They joined them on the floor.
Thembi leaned toward Sipho and said, “Today we’re getting a brand new book!”
When the reading time started, all the children listened closely.
Sipho smiled. He felt happy inside. Now he knew that reading is fun, especially when you read in your home language!

Susheela lives in Tamil Nadu.

She learnt to draw kolams from her mother.

image.alt: Girl and mother drawing kolams

pages.text: Every Pongal, she was allowed to make one kolam all by herself.

image.alt: Girl drawing a kolam and hen watching

pages.text:
Susheela loved to make kolams!

She drew them on floors and steps and walls...

image.alt: Girl drawing kolams on floors, walls and stairs

pages.text: ... on trains and on the sides of tall buildings...

image.alt: Girl drawing kolams on trains

pages.text:
... even on kites that skipped in the sky.

Everyone admired Susheela's kolams!

image.alt: Girl and boy flying kites on terrace with kolam designs

pages.text:
One day, the Air Force asked her to help them make a kolam!

Susheela told the pilots how to dip, dive and turn their planes...

image.alt: Girl and pilots with a kolam design on a paper

pages.text: ... and in minutes there was a big, beautiful and colourful kolam in the sky, that everyone in the city could see!

image.alt: Girls looking at the sky which has the design of a kolam made by planes

pages.text:
That night, Susheela stood on her terrace and looked up at the sky. She saw the stars twinkling down at her.

Where do you think Susheela will make her next kolam?

image.alt: Girl and bird looking at starry night sky with kolams

pages.text:
Know more about Kolams...

Kolams are beautiful patterns made freehand or by joining dots. People decorate the outside of their homes with kolams to welcome a new day. They are also thought to bring good luck. Traditionally, the powder used to make kolams is made out of rice flour.

Kolams are also known as Moggu, Rangoli, Chowkpurna, Alpana and Hase Chittara. What do you call a kolam in your part of the country?

In a small garden in the city, there was a big pipal tree.

A family of squirrels lived on that tree. Vikki is one member of that family who likes to talk big. His cousin, Kato had come to visit him from Far Forest.

image.alt: Pipal tree with squirrels

pages.text:
“Today we shall go on a big boat,” said Vikki to Kato.

“B... B... But, I... I...am afraid of water, I cannot swim,” mumbled Kato.

“Come on, you scrappy squirrel! With Vikki around, you need not be afraid. I have been on a boat many times.”

Vikki importantly leading the way, they reached the river.

image.alt: Squirrels talking in front of Pipal Tree

pages.text: The boat was tied to a post. So they ran up the rope, hopped into the boat, and sat curled in a corner.

image.alt: Squirrels running on a rope to a boat

pages.text:
Slowly the boat started moving up and down the river, which curled and curved through the trees. Kato saw many ducks swimming past them.

The fish put their heads out of the water and gulped a “Hello!”

Some swans majestically glided near them.

image.alt: Squirrels on a boat, seeing fishes and swans

pages.text:
They were so beautiful that Kato tried to touch one and he toppled over into the river. As he went deeper into the water, he passed some fish.

“Help! Help!” he gurgled, as he passed the boat.

image.alt: Squirrel and fishes look as another squirrel falls into water

pages.text:
Vikki did not know what to do. He just scampered from one side of the boat to the other side, shouting, “Help! Squirrel overboard!”

A swan had seen Kato fall into the water. She just put her head down in the water and picked up Kato in her beak. Then she tossed him into the boat.

image.alt: Swan with squirrel in the beak, Squirrels on the boat

pages.text:
A shivering, trembling Kato sat in a sunny corner to dry himself.

Vikki sat quietly near him. As he got warm and dry, he cheered up, “What an adventure! Wait till I tell the folks back home.”

Already he fancied himself as a sailor! A hero! Brave and adventurous!

image.alt: Squirrel thinking of a sailing squirrel

pages.text:
When the boat reached the bank, the squirrels hopped off and swaggered their way home. Kato was finding it difficult to keep his grand adventure inside his head. His head was going round and round like the boat.

He shut his eyes and fell fast asleep at the dinner table.

image.alt: Squirrels walking in the forest

One morning, Lindi found an elephant in her room.
“Look!” she called. “There’s an elephant in my room!”
“No there isn’t,” her mother called back.
“Elephants don’t live in houses. Everybody knows that.”
The elephant yawned.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_04_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
At breakfast, Lindi’s dad asked her to pass the milk.
“I can’t,” said Lindi. “The elephant drank it all.”
“There isn’t an elephant,” said her dad.
“Elephants don’t live in the city. Everybody knows that.”
The elephant burped.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_06_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
At school, the teacher grumbled, “What’s wrong with this chalkboard? It’s all wrinkly!”
“That’s not the chalkboard. That’s my elephant!” said Lindi.
“There are no elephants at school,” said the teacher. “Everybody knows that.”
The elephant ate the teacher’s sandwiches.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_07_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
At break-time, the elephant followed Lindi to the playground.
He knocked over the swings by mistake.
“Go away!” said Lindi. “You’re not real and you shouldn’t be here! Everybody knows that!”
The elephant drooped. He walked away, wiping his eyes with his trunk.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_08_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
After school, Lindi couldn’t see the elephant anywhere.
“Elephant!” she called. “Where are you?”

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_09_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
Lindi went home without him.
She felt lonely.
So she went outside, and sat on the steps, and waited.
And waited.
And waited.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_10_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
And then … she saw a trunk.
And tusks.
And ears.
The elephant was coming down the road!

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_11_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
She ran up and hugged him.
“I’m sorry,” she said. “I didn’t mean it! I know you’re real. You’re my elephant.”

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_12_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
The elephant lifted her up and put her on his back, and she rode down the street.
She waved to her neighbours.
“Hello, Mr Green! Hello, Mrs Green!”
“Look at Lindi!” said Mr Green. “How did she get up there? Maybe she grew!”
“Don’t be silly,” said Mrs Green. “Little girls don’t grow that high. Everybody knows that.”

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_13_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
The elephant took Lindi to the lake, and she slid down his trunk like it was a slide.
“Wheeeee!” she shrieked.
They played all afternoon, laughing and splashing and spraying each other with water.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_14_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text:
That night, the elephant tucked her into bed.
“Good night, Elephant,” said Lindi. “Thank you for a lovely day.”
He patted her head, and curled up to sleep outside her window.

image.alt: This picture, BD_16_the-elephant-in-the-room_english_20160323_Page_15_Image_0001.jpg, is missing or was loading too slowly.

pages.text: “Elephants are the best friends in the world,” Lindi said to herself. “Nobody knows that, except for me and my elephant.”

pages.text: Once upon a time, a little red hen was out running errands when she found a basket of corn abandoned beside the road.
She began to think about making some delicious tortillas.

“Can you help me make tortillas?” she asked her friend the goat.
But the goat did not want to help.

“Can you help me make tortillas?” she asked her friend the pig.
But the pig did not want to help.

“Can you help me make tortillas?” she asked her friend the turkey.
But the turkey did not want to help.

“Can you help me make tortillas?” she asked her friend the sheep.
But the sheep did not want to help.

“Can you help me make tortillas?” she asked her friend the duck.
But the duck did not want to help.

Finally, the little red hen gathered all her friends together.
“Please help me make tortillas!” she said. “They will be so delicious when they are ready.”
But still, none of her friends wanted to help. They all thought it would be too much work.
So the little red hen began to work all by herself. First, she cut down the tall grass to clear an area for planting.
Then she planted the corn in neat rows.
She worked hard to make sure that there were no weeds and that the plants were healthy.
A few months later, the corn was ready to harvest.
The little red hen ground the corn to make dough and cooked the tortillas on a comal.
The tortillas turned out beautifully!

When the friends of the little red hen smelled the tortillas cooking, they all came running: the goat, the pig, the turkey, the sheep, and the duck.
"Let's all eat the delicious tortillas together!" they cried.
But the little red hen said, "No! When I asked you to help me make tortillas, none of you would help. I was the only one who worked for the tortillas, and I will be the only one to eat them."
And so the little red hen ate the delicious tortillas all by herself, because we all know that to share in the harvest, we must be willing to share in the work.

books.title: The Plant Whisperer

pages.text:
Jaishree, a young engineering student, looked at her noisy machines.
“Aiyyooo!
So frustrating,” she thought.
Beep-Beep Beep
Grrrrr Grrrrr Grrrrr
Brrrrr Brrrrr Brrrrr

She missed Paati’s garden.
The garden had birds.
Trees.
Plants.
Grass.
Best of all, the garden had...

Treeni, her best friend.
Treeni’s branches were like arms, on which she climbed
and played and slept.

Jaishree called her father. “Daddy, I am going to study plants.”
Humphh!
Daddy was an engineer and didn’t like it. “I can convince him later,” Jaishree thought.
She moved to a college to study plants.

And study she did. She finished two degrees in five years. “But there are SO MANY questions that I do not have answers to.”
Do plants listen to each other?
Do plants talk to each other?
Do they fight?
Can they be friends with each other, like Treeni was mine?

Jaishree went many places in search of answers.
From New Delhi she went to New York and back to New Delhi.
Sadly, the answers were nowhere to be found.
Until she went to France. That was where she heard a story.

A lonely mustard plant could not grow properly under stress. It was small, sick and sad when the temperature was too high or too low, or when the light was too bright or too dim, or when the soil was too sandy.
But when the mustard plant had a friend nearby — another mustard plant — they both grew tall, green and happy. The mustard plants were helping each other! Alone, they were weak. Together, strong.

They helped each other, like Treeni helped little birds and squirrels.
They protected each other, like Treeni protected younger plants from harsh sunlight.

But Jaishree still had more questions than answers!
Why do plants help each other? How do plants help each other?

Jaishree thought and thought and thought. She read and read and read.
She spoke to people, helpful and unhelpful, but NOBODY had answers.

Luckily for Jaishree, mustard plants were fun to work with.
Growing them was not difficult, and she needed only one simple tool.

A paperclip!
Jaishree used a paperclip to sow 4,000 tiny seeds, one at a time.
She did this whole exercise many, many, many times.

But she didn’t get all the answers all the time. She failed and failed and failed.
She failed 21 TIMES!

Jaishree had more worries. Humans are not always as helpful as mustard plants.
She was often told wrong and unkind things.
“Women cannot do science.”
“Indians cannot do science.”
“STOP BUGGING ME,” Jaishree thought.
And she carried on with her work.

Finally, Jaishree succeeded.
“Oh yes, I have found it!”
She found that plants helped each other all the time.
She found that some mustard plants helped only similar mustard plants. Other mustard plants helped mustard plants that were not so similar.

As Jaishree knew, exciting answers always lead to more questions!
“That’s curious. Why would some plants do one thing and others do something else? Why can’t all plants help each other in the same way?”
She found that plants which grew with strangers learnt to help those strangers.
This behaviour is shaped over many many years by another curious thing called evolution.

Jaishree thought, “Imagine if we could find out which seeds to grow together so that they help each other. Wouldn’t that be fantastic?
“We could produce so many seeds in so little time with much less money!”

But what seeds grow together? How should they be grown?
Then, there are other questions too.
Are plants smart? How smart are they?
Jaishree is on a journey to find these answers. In the meanwhile, she learns every day from her helpful plants.

“If only humans helped each other more, the world would be such a wonderful place!”
What did YOU learn from plants today?

"Please Ma, may I help you make scarecrows?" asked Gauri.

Ma was tying some sticks together to make a scarecrow. She put an old shirt over the sticks, and then stuffed it with hay.

image.alt: Girl talking to lady

pages.text:
Gauri walked to the clothesline where the washed clothes were drying. She picked up a dress.

"I will dress her up in my new red frock and tie her hair with red ribbons too! She will look so lovely!"

image.alt: Girl looking at dress near clothesline

pages.text:
“You silly girl. You can't have a pretty scarecrow. Scarecrows have to scare the birds away, and so they must look scary! Like this!” said Mother, making a face and waving her arms.

Gauri giggled. “You look so funny Ma!”

image.alt: Girl laughing at lady making faces

pages.text: Mother took the scarecrows into the fields and fixed them amidst the tall stalks of grain. "There now, be good scarecrows and chase the birds away," said Gauri, patting them.

image.alt: Girl and lady making a scarecrow

pages.text:
Gauri and her mother returned to their hut.

Gauri went inside and lay on her cot.

A big yellow moon was rising, bathing the field in a soft, white glow.

image.alt: Girl looking at scarecrows in a field

pages.text:
Gauri saw a scarecrow look down at its clothes.

“Why do we always have to wear these tattered old clothes?” said a scarecrow with a sigh. “I wish we had something pretty to wear!”

“Yes, me too!” said another. The scarecrows looked around the field. Suddenly, one of them called out, “Hey, look at those lovely clothes flapping in the breeze. Why don't we wear those?”

“Oo-oo! These clothes are so pretty. Let us try them on!” said another.

image.alt: Girl looking at scarecrows through a window

pages.text: One scarecrow tried on a lovely red dress with sequins on them. It sparkled in the moonlight. She tied the pretty red ribbons that were flapping in the breeze on her straw hair. Thrilled with her new clothes she began to show them off.

image.alt: Scarecrow wearing a red dress

pages.text:
Soon, all the scarecrows were busy dressing up! They began to parade. They walked! They turned! They twisted! They twirled!

They tossed their empty mud-pot heads, and smiled their crooked mud-pot smiles. They were having a wonderful time!

image.alt: Scarecrows dancing

pages.text:
At the same time, hundreds of birds flew down to the fields. Birds here, birds there, birds everywhere. Beaks smacking! Beaks munching! Beaks chomping!

"Mmm! This is delicious!" said one, as she wiped her beak with her wing.

image.alt: Birds eating

pages.text:
“It is not everyday that we can eat in the fields, without being shooed away by the scarecrows.” The scarecrows heard this and looked around. They were horrified!

“Shoo! Be gone!” they shouted at the birds, waving their straw hands wildly, to and fro.

image.alt: Scarecrows looking at birds

pages.text:
Gauri screamed. Her mother came running.“Gauri, Gauri, what is the matter? Wake up!”

“Oh Ma, the birds! They are eating up all the grain.”

Her mother held her tight, and said, “Shh, my child! Look at the fields. They are safe! It must be a bad dream.”

image.alt: Birds on a cot

pages.text:
Gauri looked out.

She saw the scarecrows, standing just where they were placed.

image.alt: Mother and daughter

pages.text:
Oh, wait a minute, were they waving to her? She looked closer.

She saw a red ribbon fluttering on a scarecrow's hair. She blinked and looked again. Did the scarecrow just wink at her?

image.alt: Scarecrow winking at girl

books.title: When the Clouds Came Home

pages.text:
Dark clouds gather in the sky.
Lightning strikes.
Dadaji says, “It looks like it is going to rain.”
Children dance and sing, waiting for the rains.

Raindrops begin to fall.
Trees sway, birds flap their wings and fly home.
The animals run helter-skelter.
The parched soil is soaked.
The farmers pick up their ploughs.
It is time to plant. It is time to sow.

The rain lashes down.
The streams, the lakes and the rivers overflow.
The village is lush. It is green.
The farmers go to the fields, the fisherfolk to the river.
The peacock dances joyfully.

The rice is ripe. The rice is gold.
The farmers go to the fields, sickle in hand.
To cut. To gather. To harvest.
Some take the grains home to cook. Some store it for another time.
It is time to feast.

Everyone is busy. Everyone is happy.
The village is full of life.
A story as old as the hills.

The village grows and changes, bit by bit.
The villagers have to go to the forests dark and deep.
First to gather the twigs, then the sticks, then the branches.
To cook. To build homes.

People need space. They need more.
More of everything.

Contractors enter the village.
Trucks carry away the trees.
The forest grows smaller. It is quieter.
There are fewer animals.
The birds don’t sing as much.

Things are changing fast.
The village is now a town.
There is noise and there is smoke.

The hills lie bare.
The trees have disappeared.
There is no rain.
The streams stop flowing.
The villagers now have to walk for miles to get water.

The villagers wait for the rains.
They look up, searching for rain clouds.
But there’s only the sun. Blazing mighty and fierce, across a dusty sky.
The few animals and birds are thirsty, looking for water.
The rivers have dried up.
The farmers sit silent. They are angry.

“We need trees. We need hills.”
Young and old, everyone begins planting trees.
The children help dig the soil. They plant the saplings.

Slowly, the hills are lush, they are green.
Rain clouds are spotted in the sky.
The birds and animals return home.
The farmers are ready to go back to the fields.
The fisherfolk, to the river.
Like the peacock, they all dance with joy.
